cells.tense: You are here with the tools, and what you make comes out finished.
cells.ask: Show one person the last thing you finished, and let it stand without adjusting it.
cells.core:
The same chair, the same hour, the thing getting a little truer each time. That's how it goes — not one big push but reps, kept lit by attention instead of flash. What you work with now lives in your hands. It shows there before it shows in any plan.

The strength underneath is quiet. It holds through the long middle stretch when nothing looks different yet, and it doesn't need the middle to feel good. Keep it fed and it keeps feeding the work. What you can hand on next is the staying itself — the way you remain with a thing past the interesting part.
cells.sheetLine: You show up, keep the reps going, and the work gets true.
cells.verb: building skill through repeated reps until the work stands finished
cells.place: the practice room, where skill is built by reps

cells.tense: You are grinding toward a version that will finally be done, and the future is doing the work.
cells.ask: Stop at a set count today, not at a feeling of done.
cells.core:
You're rehearsing the finished version in your head while the current one sits half-formed. More reps, more polish, another pass — as if the last one today might lock it into place. The practice in front of you is real. The bracing is the part that isn't practicing.

What balance looks like here is choosing the next rep from a clear head, not from the pressure that says stopping means falling behind. Direction comes back when you let one session be enough. That's the cost of keeping this steady: some days you close the book while it's still rough. The rep you do counts even when nobody sees it.

cells.tense: The practice has gone quiet, and you're still standing at a door you already walked through.
cells.ask: Put twenty minutes into one small piece today, before anything else gets your attention.
cells.core:
The tools are still where you left them. What's thin isn't ability — it's the small light you used to keep on with daily attention. Without it, skill has nothing to grow in, and the quiet looks like the whole story. It isn't. The reps you already own haven't gone anywhere; they're just not being added to.

What's there instead of the work is plain looking at what is. Don't force feeling into the quiet; let that looking come first. Start small enough that nothing has to be answered for: one pass, one drill, one page. The strength here isn't in the finish — it's in coming back and picking it up again. Doing that once today is the whole move.

cells.tense: You already run the disciplined practice, and you keep calling it just keeping busy.
cells.ask: Name one skill you built by your own effort, out loud, as yours.
cells.core:
Look at what's built: the reps you did when no one asked, the skill that now lives in your hands. You did that. The way you talk, it sounds like it happened on its own — fine, nothing to claim. The making moved through you on purpose, and the telling hasn't caught up.

What holds that together is simple: noticing something clearly before naming it. Use it. Acknowledge one thing as your work and let that be enough for the moment — no need to prove it, just to say it. The strength here holds without pushing and gives the credit back where it belongs.
cells.sheetLine: You built that practice. Calling it nothing doesn't make it less yours.

attempts.check: The record says nothing about who taught this person to distrust finish, and the Too Little cell must not invent a room or a loss behind the stopped work. The reader could fairly say 'my practice isn't starved, I just don't care about finishing,' and the ask still holds because naming what the reps are for is useful either way — the cull of small pieces stands whether or not the diagnosis of the stopping is right. The line that would serve me more than the person is any version of 'you were never taught to finish.' I cut it; the cell locates the lack and stays inside it.
